evidence.label: Near Inclusions of von Neumann Algebras Without Small Spatial Embeddings
Close Separable C*-Algebras Without Spatial Conjugacy

headline: Proves, with a Lean check, that close von Neumann algebras are conjugate by a unitary near the identity, uniformly.
scope: Unital von Neumann algebras on any complex Hilbert space, plus two companion counterexamples for one-sided near inclusions and separable C*-algebras.
plain: Two operator algebras on the same space are close if every element of one is near some element of the other. Kadison and Kastler asked in 1972 whether close von Neumann algebras must be rotated copies of each other by a nearly trivial unitary. This paper proves yes, with a tolerance that works for every algebra at once, and Lean checks it. Two companion papers claim the answer fails for one-sided near inclusions and for separable C*-algebras.
doesNot: This does not extend to C*-algebras, where a companion paper claims close separable algebras need not be conjugate at all.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.firstStepBy: Richard Kadison and Daniel Kastler, perturbation problem for operator algebras
scorecard.significanceWhy: It settles the strong Kadison–Kastler conjecture, a central perturbation problem open for over fifty years.

explanation:
Take the 2-by-2 matrices that are zero off the diagonal. Call this algebra M. Rotate the plane by an angle of 0.1 radians, using a rotation matrix u. The rotated algebra N = uMu* is a tilted copy of M. The rotation moves vectors only a little: the distance from u to the identity is 2 sin(0.05), about 0.09996. The projection diag(1, 0) in M and its rotated copy in N differ by sin(0.1), about 0.0998. Every unit-size element of M has a partner in N within twice 0.09996. So a small unitary makes nearby algebras.

The Kadison–Kastler question runs the other way. Measure how far apart two algebras are by comparing their unit balls, the elements of size at most one. This Kadison–Kastler distance was introduced in 1972[1]. If two von Neumann algebras on one space are very close, must one be a slightly rotated copy of the other? A von Neumann algebra is an algebra of operators closed under adjoints and under weak limits. Early results covered type I algebras and then amenable algebras[2]. Some non-amenable factors were later shown to be stable too. The obstacle was the general case: algebras of every type, with no structure to lean on.

This paper proves the uniform answer. For every ε > 0 there is a δ > 0 that works for every Hilbert space and every pair of algebras. If their distance is below δ, some unitary u with ‖u − I‖ < ε carries one onto the other[3]. The tolerance does not depend on the algebras, their type or their representations[4].

Two companion papers mark the edges. The second looks at one-sided near inclusions, where M is only nearly inside N. It answers negatively the unrestricted question of whether small near inclusions come from small unitaries[5]. Its examples do have unitary embeddings, but every one stays a fixed distance from the identity[6]. The third turns to C*-algebras, which need only be closed in norm. It claims arbitrarily close separable C*-algebras that no unitary can conjugate at all[7]. Those two algebras have the same von Neumann closure[7]. It gives no counterexample for von Neumann algebras[8].

How sure is this? A computer proof checker called Lean has a formal proof of the main theorem. It covers all unital von Neumann algebras on any complex Hilbert space, with δ depending only on ε. The two companion counterexamples are not part of that Lean statement. No specialist review of the papers has been published.
hypeCheck: Landmark: it settles the strong Kadison–Kastler conjecture, and Lean formally checks the main theorem. The two companion counterexamples have no Lean check, and no specialist review is published.

glossary.meaning: An algebra of operators on a Hilbert space, closed under adjoints and under weak limits.
An algebra of operators closed under adjoints and under limits in the operator norm, a stronger kind of limit.
An operator that preserves lengths and angles, like a rotation; it is invertible with inverse equal to its adjoint.
How far apart two operator algebras are, measured by how well each unit ball approximates the other.
The elements of an algebra whose operator norm is at most one.
A one-sided closeness: every unit-size element of M is near some element of N.
A property of algebras that allows averaging arguments; it fails for many large algebras.
Having a countable dense subset, a mild size limit.
